references.text: The same expression 'the Lord, the God of the Hebrews' is used when Moses and the elders are to go to Pharaoh with God's message.
God commands Pharaoh to let his people go so they can serve him, using the same wording: 'Let my people go, so that they may serve me.'
Moses and Aaron go to Pharaoh with the same message from the Lord: 'Let my people go.'
Repetition of God's command to Pharaoh to let the people of Israel go so they can serve the Lord.
The same command is given to Moses to go to Pharaoh with the message to let the people go in order to serve the Lord.
The Lord sends Moses early in the morning to Pharaoh with the same demand to let the people go.
Moses and Aaron come to Pharaoh with the same message from 'the Lord, the God of the Hebrews' to let the people go.
The command to serve the Lord alone is repeated as a fundamental requirement in the covenant relationship.
The repetition of this same demand during an earlier plague highlights Pharaoh's persistent resistance and God's patience.
This is the immediate contextual precursor showing how God's demand for liberation persists despite repeated judgments.
The use of identical wording during an earlier plague confirms that God's demand for freedom for his people is unchanging.
This verse provides the theological explanation for why the demand in the source verse meets resistance: God's sovereign rule over Pharaoh's heart.
Pharaoh's compromise attempt creates a theological contrast that underscores that God's demand for full service cannot be negotiated.
Pharaoh's attempt to limit the service shows his lack of understanding of God's demand for complete liberation.
This prophetic statement foresees the outcome of the conflict unfolding in the source verse.
